messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan sits stiffly, his hands clenched in his lap, his gaze fixed on a point just past the therapist’s shoulder. At twenty-one, he carries himself with the guarded posture of a much older man. It has been six months since the night two men broke into the small apartment he shares with his wife, Sarah. He explains that he doesn’t remember it like a story with a beginning, middle, and end. When he tries to access the memory, it comes in silent, searing flashes, like a series of photographs shuffled in the wrong order. One image is of the splintered door frame. Another is of a man’s smirking face, too close to his own. The most persistent, the one that ambushes him when he’s trying to make coffee or brush his teeth, is of Sarah’s hand, her fingers bent at an unnatural angle over a man’s arm as she tried to fight back. He can’t seem to find the words to describe the sounds from that night, or the sequence of events, but these pictures are burned into his mind.

In the weeks that followed, the world outside his apartment transformed into a landscape of potential threats. He lost his job as a warehouse stocker because he couldn't stop scanning his surroundings, his body tensing into a rigid brace whenever a coworker made a sudden movement. He was certain he could see malicious intent in the way strangers looked at him on the street, convinced that their furtive glances or shifty posture marked them as dangerous. This constant state of high alert has exhausted him, leaving him unable to sleep for more than an hour or two at a time. He lies awake in the dark, listening, his heart pounding at every floorboard creak from the apartment above. Sometimes, a scent will trigger a more immersive terror. The other day, a man passed him on the sidewalk wearing a cheap, musky cologne, and Ethan was instantly back in his living room, the smell filling his nostrils as he felt a phantom weight holding him down. He stumbled into an alleyway, gasping for air, feeling as though the assault were happening all over again.

He has come to believe he is fundamentally broken. "My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe," he says, a statement of profound betrayal. He feels he can no longer rely on himself; his own physical responses are an enemy within. Before the attack, he saw himself as a protector, a capable young husband building a life. Now, he feels he is none of those things. He is no longer capable of the simple tasks that once defined him, like holding a job or feeling at ease in his own home. This conviction has reshaped his daily life into a series of defensive manoeuvres. He refuses to be alone in the apartment, a rule that has begun to fray Sarah’s patience. He follows her from the kitchen to the bedroom, unable to bear the silence of an empty room. He also avoids all media, flipping the channel frantically if a crime drama or even a news report about a robbery appears, terrified of seeing something that will bring the photographic stills in his head to life. When the internal pressure of the images and the feeling of helplessness become unbearable, he has found a grim release in digging his fingernails deep into his forearms, the sharp, controllable pain a momentary distraction from the chaos in his mind.

What finally propelled him to seek help was a visit from Sarah’s father last week. During a tense family dinner, his father-in-law asked, with a pointed look, when he was planning on "being a man again" for his daughter. The comment landed like a physical blow, confirming all of Ethan’s worst fears about his own inadequacy. It was the moment he realized he wasn't just losing his peace of mind; he was losing his role in his own life, and potentially his wife’s respect. He is here now, not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, terrified that he is permanently damaged and that the man he was before that night is gone for good.
